text:
Marathon Petroleum's stock has fallen about 0.4% today, continuing a steady decline over the past week that has wiped out most of its modest two-week gains. The pullback comes despite oil prices sitting near six-month highs—Brent crude is at $116 per barrel—driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East and Houthi attacks on regional energy infrastructure. For a refiner, this is counterintuitive at first: higher crude oil prices typically squeeze refining margins (the profit on turning crude into gasoline and diesel) because refiners' input costs rise faster than they can pass those costs to consumers. The U.S. refinery sector is running at 93.4% capacity, already near peak utilization, leaving little room to boost output and capture upside from the price spike.

The broader context here is that energy markets are pricing in geopolitical risk rather than strong fundamentals. Gasoline and diesel inventories remain relatively healthy (205 million and 104 million barrels respectively), so there's no supply crunch driving demand for refined products—the oil price move is about Middle East conflict and supply threats, not refinery strength.
